text: 壽永三年正月一日、院の御所は大膳大夫成忠が宿所、六條西洞院なれば、御所の體しかるべからずとて、禮儀行はるべきにあらねば拜禮もなし。院の拜禮無りければ、内裏の小朝拜もおこなはれず。平家は讃岐國八島の磯におくり迎へて、年のはじめなれども元旦元三の儀式事宜からず、主上わたらせ給へども、節會も行はれず、四方拜もなし。はらか魚も奏せず。吉野のくずも參らず。「世亂れたりしかども都にてはさすがかくは無りし者を。」とぞ、各宣ひあはれける。青陽の春も來り、浦吹く風もやはらかに、日影も長閑に成行けど、唯平家の人々は、いつも氷に閉籠られたる心地して、寒苦鳥に異ならず。東岸西岸の柳遲速を交へ、南枝北枝の梅開落已に異にして、花の朝月の夜、詩歌管絃、鞠、小弓、扇合、繪合、草盡、蟲盡、樣々興有し事ども思出で語りつゞけて、永き日を暮しかね給ふぞ哀なる。

annotation.translation: In the first day of the first month of the third year of Juei, since the Emperor's palace was at the residence of the Great Food Master Naritada, located at Rokujō Nishi-dōin, the Emperor's presence was not appropriate, and since proper ceremonies could not be performed, there was no prostration. Since the Emperor did not prostrate, the small morning prostration at the Inner Palace was not carried out. The Taira escorted and welcomed him to the shore of Hishima in Sanuki Province; though it was the beginning of the year, the ceremonies for the first day of the first month were not properly held, and even though the Emperor arrived, no seasonal festivals were performed, and there was no prostration to the four directions. No hara fish was presented. No Yoshino kuzu arrived. "Although the world is in turmoil, such a situation has never occurred in the capital," each declared with sorrow. Spring of the clear sun arrived, the wind blowing from the sea became gentle, and the shadows of the day grew peaceful, yet the people of the Taira always felt as if they were imprisoned in ice, no different from a cold and bitter bird. The willows on the eastern and western shores alternated in their speed of budding, and the plum blossoms on the southern and northern branches had already begun to open and fall; on mornings of flowers and nights of the moon, they recalled and continued to speak of poetry, music, ball games, small bows, fan games, painting contests, grass games, and insect games, various pastimes, and could not pass the long days; how mournful it is.

text: 同正月十一日、木曾左馬頭義仲院參して、平家追討の爲に、西國へ發向すべき由奏聞す。同十三日既に門出と聞えし程に、東國より前兵衞佐頼朝、木曾が狼藉鎭んとて、數萬騎の軍兵を差上せられける。既に美濃國伊勢國に著と聞えしかば、木曾大に驚き、宇治勢田の橋を引いて、軍兵どもを分ち遣す。折節勢も無りけり。勢田の橋は、大手なればとて、今井四郎兼平、八百餘騎で差遣す。宇治橋へは、仁科、高梨、山田次郎、五百餘騎でつかはす。芋洗へは、伯父の志太三郎先生義教、三百餘騎で向けり。東國より攻上る大手の大將軍は、蒲の御曹司範頼、搦手の大將軍は、九郎御曹司義經、むねとの大名三十餘人、都合其勢六萬餘騎とぞ聞えし。其比鎌倉殿にいけずき摺墨といふ名馬あり。いけずきをば梶原源太景頻に望み申けれども、鎌倉殿「自然の事あらん時、物具して頼朝がのるべき馬なり。する墨も劣ぬ名馬ぞ。」とて、梶原にはする墨をこそ給だりけれ。

annotation.translation: On the eleventh day of the same first month, he visited the residence of Saemon-no-jo Ieyasu of Kiso to report that he should set out for the Western Provinces to suppress the Taira clan. By the thirteenth day, it was reported that he had already departed; meanwhile, from the Eastern Provinces, Maeda-no-suke Yoritomo had dispatched tens of thousands of cavalry troops to quell Kiso's lawlessness. Upon hearing that they had already reached Mino and Ise provinces, Kiso was greatly alarmed, drew up the bridge at Uji-Seta, and dispatched his troops in divisions. At that time, there was a lack of manpower. Since the Seta bridge was the main route, Iwai no Shiro Kanehira was sent with over eight hundred cavalry. At the Uji Bridge, Shinoda, Takanashi, and Yamada no Jiro were sent with over five hundred cavalry. At Imashiki, his uncle, Shida no Saburo Choshu Yoshinori, was sent with over three hundred cavalry. The main general advancing from the Eastern Provinces was Lord Hachiman's son Noriyori; the rear general was Lord Hachiman's son Yoshitsune. There were over thirty great lords, including Munenoto, bringing the total force to over sixty thousand cavalry, as reported. At that time, in Kamakura, there was a famous horse named Ikezuki, a polished black horse. Yoritomo requested the Ikezuki from Kajiwara no Genta Kagehisa, but Kamakura said, 'When the time comes, it is a horse that should be ridden by Yoritomo himself. Even the Suruzumi is not an inferior famous horse.' Thus, he gave the Suruzumi to Kajiwara.

text: 佐々木四郎高綱が暇申に參たりけるに、鎌倉殿如何思食されけん、「所望の者はいくらもあれども、存知せよ。」とて、いけずきをば佐々木に給ぶ。佐々木畏て申けるは「高綱此御馬で、宇治川の眞先渡し候べし。宇治河で死で候ときこしめし候はゞ、人に先をせられてけりと思食し候へ。未だ生て候と聞食され候はゞ、定めて先陣はしつらんものをと思食され候へ。」とて、御前を罷り立つ。參會したる大名小名皆「荒凉の申樣哉。」とささやきあへり。

annotation.translation: When Sasaki Shiro Takatsuna came to take his leave, the Kamakura Lord inquired, 'Although there are many things one might desire, I know them.' Then, he gave the troublesome matter to Sasaki. Sasaki, with reverence, replied, 'Takatsuna should cross the Uji River at its very forefront on this magnificent horse. If it is heard that you died at the Uji River, you will think, 'I was outdone by others.' If it is heard that you are still alive, you will surely think, 'I must have been the vanguard.' With these words, he took his leave from the presence. All the great and minor lords who were present whispered, 'What a desolate situation!'

text: 各鎌倉を立て、足柄を歴て行もあり、箱根にかゝる人もあり、思ひ／＼に上る程に、駿河國浮島原にて梶原源太景季、高き所に打上り、暫しひかへて、多の馬共を見ければ、思ひ／＼の鞍置て、いろ／＼の鞦かけ、或は乘り口に引かせ、或はもろ口に引かせ、幾千萬といふ數を知らず、引き通し／＼しける中にも、景季が給はたるするすみに、勝る馬こそ無かりけれと、嬉しう思ひて見る處に、いけずきとおぼしき馬こそ出來たれ。

annotation.translation: Each [person] set up a Kamakura, some went through Ashigara, and some came to Hakone; as they climbed in various ways, at Ukishima Plain in Suruga Province, Kajiwara Gen'ta Kagetoki, having climbed to a high place, waited a while, and when he saw many horses, he put on various saddles, hung various bridles, had some led by the reins in front, had others led by the reins at the side, not knowing the number of thousands and tens of thousands; even while drawing them out in various ways, among those, there was not a horse superior to the one given by Kagetoki, but in the place where he thought happily and looked, a horse that seemed unsuitable appeared.

text: 金覆輪の鞍置て、小總の鞦懸け、白沫かませ、舎人あまた附たりけれども、猶引もためず躍らせて出きたり。梶原源太打寄て、「其れは誰が御馬ぞ。」「佐々木殿の御馬候。」其時梶原「安からぬ者なり。おなじやうにめしつかはるゝ景季を佐々木におぼしめしかへられけるこそ遺恨なれ。都へ上て木曾殿の御内に四天王と聞ゆる、今井、樋口、楯、根井に組んで死ぬるか、然らずば西國へ向うて、一人當千と聞る平家の侍共と軍して死なんとこそ思つれども、此御氣色では、それも詮なし。爰で佐々木に引組み刺違へ、好い侍二人死で兵衞佐殿に損とらせ奉らん。」とつぶやいてこそ待懸たれ。佐々木四郎は何心もなく歩せて出來たり。梶原押竝べてやくむ、向うざまにやあて落すと思ひけるが、先詞を懸けり。「いかに佐々木殿、いけずき給はらせ給てさうな。」と言ひければ、佐々木「あはれ此仁も内々所望すると聞し物を。」ときと思ひ出して、「さ候へばこそ此御大事にのぼり候が、定て宇治勢田の橋をばひいて候らん。乘て河渡すべき馬はなし。いけずきを申さばやとは思へども、梶原殿の申されけるにも御許れないと承はる間、まして高綱が申すにもよも給らじと思つゝ後日には如何なる御勘當も有ばあれと存じて、曉立んとての夜、舎人に心をあはせて、さしも御秘藏候いけずきを盗みすまいて上りさうはいかに。」と言ひければ、梶原此詞に腹がゐて、「ねたい、さらば景季も竊むべかりける者を。」とて、どと笑て退にけり。

annotation.translation: With a gold-rimmed saddle, a small stirrup hung, covered in white foam, though many pages attended, he did not hesitate to lead out, leaping forth. Kajiwara Gen'ichi approached and said, "Whose horse is that?" "It is Lord Sasaki's horse," he replied. At that time Kajiwara said, "He is a dangerous man. There is deep resentment because Lord Kagekiyo, who served in the same manner, was thought to be Lord Sasaki and sent away. I thought that I should go up to the capital, join the Four Heavenly Kings known to be in Lord Kiso's household—Imai, Higuchi, Tate, and Nee—and die together, or else, if not, head to the Western Provinces and fight with the Heike warriors known as 'one man against a thousand' and die. But with this expression of yours, that is no longer possible. Here, let us challenge Sasaki to a duel and kill two fine warriors, thereby causing harm to Lord Emon Sa." Mumbling thus, he waited. Sasaki Shiro, without any thought, walked forth. Kajiwara pressed close, intending to strike him down as he passed, but the first words were spoken first. "How so, Lord Sasaki, you are too harsh." When he said this, Sasaki, thinking "Ah, I heard that such an inner wish was desired," suddenly recalled, "Since that is so, I have come to this great matter; surely I will cross Uji-Seta Bridge. There is no horse fit to ride across the river. Though I thought to speak of harshness, yet since it is understood that Lord Kajiwara will not permit it, much less will Lord Takatsuna grant it, thinking that some punishment may come on a later day, I resolved to rise at dawn, coordinating with the pages, to steal this hidden harshness that was so carefully guarded and come forth. How is it?" When he said this, Kajiwara's anger subsided, saying, "How pitiful; then Kagekiyo could have stolen it as well." And he laughed loudly and withdrew.

text: 佐々木四郎が給はたる御馬は、黒栗毛なる馬の、究めて太う逞いが、馬をも人をも傍をはらて食ければ、生食と附られたり。八寸の馬とぞ聞えし。梶原が給たる摺墨も、究めて太う逞きが、誠に黒かりければ、するすみとは附けられたり。何れも劣らぬ名馬なり。

annotation.translation: The imperial horse given by Sasaki Shiro was a black chestnut horse, extremely fat and strong; since it ate people and horses alike by driving them aside, it was called 'Nikushoku' (Flesh-Eater). It was said to be the 'Hassun' horse. The surizumi (polished ink) horse given by Kajiwara was also extremely fat and strong, but since it was truly black, it was called 'Suruzumi'. Both were famous horses without equal.

text: 尾張國より大手搦手二手にわかてせめ上る。大手の大將軍、蒲御曹司範頼、相伴ふ人々、武田太郎、加賀見次郎、一條次郎、板垣三郎、稻毛三郎、榛谷四郎、熊谷次郎、猪俣小平六を先として、都合其勢三萬五千餘騎、近江國、野路、篠原にぞつきにける。搦手の大將軍は、九郎御曹司義經同く伴ふ人々、安田三郎、大内太郎、畠山庄司次郎、梶原源太、佐々木四郎、糟屋藤太、澁谷右馬允、平山武者所を始として、都合其勢二萬五千餘騎、伊賀國を經て、宇治橋のつめにぞ押寄せたる。宇治も勢田も橋を引き、水の底には亂杭打て大綱張り、逆茂木つないで流し懸たり。比は睦月廿日餘の事なれば、比良の高峯、志賀の山、昔ながらの雪も消え、谷々の氷打解て、水は折節増りたり。白浪おびたゞしう漲り落ち、瀬枕大きに瀧鳴て、逆卷く水も疾かりけり。夜は既にほの％＼と明行けど、河霧深く立籠て、馬の毛も、鎧の毛もさだかならず。爰に大將軍九郎御曹司、河の端に進み出で、水の面を見渡して、人々の心を見んとや思はれけん、「如何せん淀芋洗へや回るべき、水の落足をや待べき。」と宣へば、畠山は其比はいまだ生年廿一に成けるが、進出でて申けるは、「鎌倉にて能々此河の御沙汰は候ひしぞかし。知召さぬ海河の俄に出來ても候はばこそ。此河は近江の水海の末なれば、待とも／＼水ひまじ。橋をば又誰か渡いて參らすべき。治承の合戰に、足利又太郎忠綱は、鬼神でわたしけるか。重忠瀬蹈仕らん。」とて、丹の黨を宗として、五百餘騎ひし／＼と轡を竝ぶる處に、平等院の丑寅、橘の小島が崎より、武者二騎引かけ引かけ出來たり。一騎は梶原源太景季、一騎は佐々木四郎高綱也。人目には何とも見えざりけれども、内々先に心をかけたりければ、梶原は佐々木に一段許ぞ進だる。佐々木四郎、「此河は西國一の大河ぞや。腹帶の延て見えさうぞ。しめ給へ。」と言はれて梶原さもあるらんとや思ひけん、左右の鎧を踏すかし、手綱を馬のゆがみに捨て、腹帶を解てぞ縮めたりける。その間に佐々木は、つと馳ぬいて、河へさとぞ打入たる。梶原謀れぬとや思ひけん、やがて續て打入たり。「いかに佐々木殿、高名せうとて不覺し給ふな。水の底には大綱あるらん。」といひければ、佐々木、太刀を拔き、馬の足に懸りける大綱共をふつ／＼と打切打切、いけずきといふ世一の馬には乘たりけり、宇治川はやしといへども一文字にさと渡いて、向への岸に打上る。梶原が乘たりける摺墨は、河中よりのだめ形に押流されて遙の下より打上げたり。佐々木鐙蹈張立上り、大音聲を揚て名乘りけるは、「宇多天皇より九代の後胤、佐々木三郎秀義が四男、佐々木四郎高綱、宇治川の先陣ぞや。吾と思はん人々は高綱に組めや。」とておめいてかく。畠山五百餘騎で軈て渡す。向への岸より、山田次郎が放つ矢に、畠山馬の額を篦ぶかに射させて弱れば、河中より弓杖を突て下立たり。岩浪甲の手先へ颯と押上けれども事ともせず。水の底を潜て、向の岸へぞ著にける。上らむとすれば後に物こそむずと引へたれ。「誰そ。」と問へば、「重親。」と答ふ。「いかに大串か。」「さ候。」大串の次郎は、畠山には烏帽子子にてぞありける。「餘に水が疾うて、馬は押流され候ぬ。力及ばで著參らせて候。」と言ひければ、「いつも和殿原は、重忠が樣なる者にこそ助られむずれ。」と云ふまゝに、大串を提て岸の上へぞ投上たる。投上られて、たゝ直て、「武藏國の住人大串次郎重親、宇治河の先陣ぞや。」とぞ名乘たる。敵も御方も是を聞いて一度にどとぞ笑ける。其後畠山乘替に乘て打上る。魚綾の直垂に緋威の鎧著て、連錢葦毛なる馬に、金覆輪の鞍置て乘たる、敵の眞先にぞ進だるを「爰にかくるは如何なる人ぞ。名乘れや。」と言ひければ、「木曾殿の家の子に、長瀬判官代重綱。」と名乘る。畠山今日の軍神祝はんとて、押竝てむずと捕て引落し、頸ねぢ切て、本田次郎が鞍のとつけにこそ附させけれ。是を始て、木曾殿の方より宇治橋固たる勢も、暫さゝへてふせぎけれども、東國の大勢渡いて攻ければ、散散に懸成され、木幡山、伏見を指いてぞ落行ける。勢田をば稻毛三郎重成が計らひにて、田上供御瀬をこそ渡しけれ。

annotation.translation: From the province of Owari, the rear guard advanced in two divisions. The great general of the main force, Prince Fujiwara no Noriyori, accompanied by his retinue—Taira Taro, Kagami Jiro, Ichijo Jiro, Itagaki Saburo, Inaba Saburo, Kurihara Shiro, Kumagai Jiro, Inomata Kogoro—numbering altogether thirty-five thousand five hundred or more horsemen, arrived at Noji and Shinohara in the province of Omi. The great general of the rear guard, Prince Fujiwara no Yoshitsune, accompanied by his retinue—Yasuda Saburo, Ouchi Taro, Hatakeyama Sanji Jiro, Kajiwara Genta, Sasaki Shiro, Kasuya Todai, Shibuya Umonosuke, Hirayama Mushashokoro—numbering altogether twenty-five thousand five hundred or more horsemen, crossed the province of Iga and pressed toward the blockade at Uji Bridge. At Uji and Seto, the bridges were drawn up, stakes were driven into the riverbed, thick ropes were stretched, and interlaced with thorn fences to block the current. This was a few days after the twentieth day of the first month; the high peaks of Hira and the mountains of Shiga, their ancient snows having melted, the ice in the valleys had thawed, and the water had risen at the season. White waves surged and fell in great abundance; the rapids roared loudly, and the swirling currents were swift. Although the night was already faintly bright, the river mist hung thick, obscuring both the horses' coats and the armor. Here the great general, Prince Fujiwara no Yoshitsune, advanced to the riverbank, gazed upon the water, and, thinking to gauge his men's hearts, said, "How shall we cross? Shall we wait for the water to recede?" Hearing this, Hatakeyama, who was still twenty-one years of age, stepped forward and said, "In Kamakura, I had thoroughly heard of this river. Had a sudden surge appeared in the sea or river without warning, I would have been prepared. But this river is the outlet of Omi's waters; even if we wait, the water will not cease. Who else could cross the bridge? In the Battle of Jisho, Ashikaga Mata Taro Tadayasu crossed like a god or demon. I shall leap into the river and wade across." Taking this as his lead, the Dan faction, with over five hundred horsemen, formed their ranks side by side. From the ushi-tora (northeast) direction of Byodo-in, and from the promontory of Tachibana's small island, two mounted warriors emerged, one after another. One was Kajiwara Genta Kagetoki; the other, Sasaki Shiro Takatsuna. Though invisible to the enemy's eyes, they had secretly prepared their hearts beforehand, and Kajiwara advanced slightly ahead of Sasaki. Sasaki Shiro said, "This river is the greatest river in the Western Provinces; the belt of my abdomen seems to be stretching. Fasten it tightly." Kajiwara, thinking to comply, stepped back, trampling on his armor's sides, cast his reins onto the horse's flank, and loosened and tightened his belt. In the meantime, Sasaki suddenly galloped and plunged into the river. Kajiwara, thinking Sasaki had acted without a plan, immediately followed, plunging in after him. "How so, Lord Sasaki! Do not be caught unawares out of desire for fame! There must be thick ropes at the riverbed!" he cried. Sasaki drew his sword, cut through the thick ropes that had been fastened to his horse's legs, and mounted a horse renowned throughout the world as "Ikezuki." Though the Uji River was swift, he crossed it in a single line, reaching the opposite bank. Kajiwara's horse, the Surisumi, was pushed downstream in a tangled mass from the river's center and cast up far below. Sasaki stood up on his stirrups, raised his voice, and proclaimed, "I am Sasaki Shiro Takatsuna, the fourth son of Sasaki Saburo Hideyoshi, a descendant of Emperor Uda through nine generations! I take the vanguard at Uji River! All who think of me, join with Takatsuna!" Then he rode forth. Hatakeyama and his five hundred horsemen soon crossed. From the opposite bank, a spear was shot by Yamada Jiro, striking Hatakeyama's horse on its forehead; weakened, Hatakeyama leaped from the river with a bow-staff and stood firm. He was pushed up by Iwanami's vanguard, but suffered no harm. He dove beneath the water and reached the opposite bank. When he tried to climb up, something was pulled back from behind. "Who is it?" he asked. "Shigechika," came the reply. "How about the great Otsugi?" "Indeed," replied Otsugi. Otsugi no Jiro was a page to Hatakeyama. "The water is too swift; my horse was swept away. I could not exert enough strength to reach the shore." Hearing this, Hatakeyama said, "It is always a man like Shigechika who should be saved." As he spoke, he lifted Otsugi and threw him onto the bank. Thrown up, Otsugi immediately stood straight and proclaimed, "I am Otsugi no Jiro Shigechika, a resident of Musashi Province, taking the vanguard at the Uji River!" Both enemy and ally heard this and burst into laughter at once. Afterward, Hatakeyama, changing his horse, rode up. Wearing a red-laced hakama and a crimson-lacquered armor, mounted on a chestnut horse with linked-chain reins and a gold-rimmed saddle, he advanced to the forefront of the enemy. "Who is hiding here? Name yourself!" they shouted. "I am Nagase no Kanjo Shigenaga, son of Lord Kiso," he replied. Hatakeyama, wishing to celebrate the day's military god, rushed forward, caught him with difficulty, pulled him down, twisted his neck, and attached him to the saddle of Honda no Jiro. From that moment on, even the forces guarding Uji Bridge from Lord Kiso's side, though momentarily holding their ground, were scattered and broken by the overwhelming forces of the Eastern Provinces. They retreated, pointing toward Kataba Mountain and Fushimi. As for Seto, Inaba Saburo Shigenari arranged for the crossing at Tanagami no Goiso.

text: 軍破れにければ、鎌倉殿へ飛脚をもて、合戰の次第を記し申されけるに、鎌倉殿先づ御使に、「佐々木は如何に。」と御尋有ければ、「宇治川の眞先候。」と申す。日記を披いて御覽ずれば、「宇治川の先陣、佐々木四郎高綱、二陣梶原源太景季。」とこそ書れたれ。

annotation.translation: Since the army was defeated, a messenger was sent to the Kamakura Lord with a written account of the battle's proceedings. The Kamakura Lord first asked his envoy, 'How about Sasaki?' Upon being told, 'He was at the forefront at Uji River,' the Lord opened the diary and read it, which stated, 'The vanguard at Uji River was Sasaki Shiro Takatsuna; the second rank was Kajiwara Genta Kagetoki.'

text: 宇治勢田破れぬと聞えしかば、木曾左馬頭最後の暇申さんとて、院の御所六條殿へ馳參る。御所には法皇を始め參せて公卿殿上人「世は只今失せなんず。如何せん。」とて手を握り立てぬ願もましまさず。木曾門前まで參たれども、東國の勢、既に河原迄責入たる由聞えしかば、さいて奏する旨もなくて、取てかへす。六條高倉なる所に始めて見そめたる女房のおはしければ、其へ打いり、最後の名殘惜まんとて、とみに出もやらざりけり。今參したりける越後中太家光と云ふ者有り、「如何にかうは打解て渡せ給候ぞ。御敵既に河原まで攻入て候に、犬死せさせ給なんず。」と申けれども、猶出でもやらざりければ、「さ候はば、先づ先き立參せて、死出の山でこそ待參せ候はめ。」とて、腹掻切てぞ死にける。木曾殿「我をすゝむる自害にこそ。」とて、やがて打立けり。上野國の住人那波太郎廣純を先として、其勢百騎ばかりには過ざりけり。六條河原に打出で見れば、東國の勢と覺くて、先三十騎計出來たり。其中に武者二騎進んだり。一騎は鹽屋五郎惟廣、一騎は勅使河原五三郎有直也。鹽屋が申けるは、「後陣の勢をや待つべき。」勅使河原が申けるは、「一陣破ぬれば殘黨全からず、唯懸よ。」とて、をめいてかく。木曾は今日を限りと戰かへば、東國の勢は、我討取んとぞ進ける。

annotation.translation: When it was heard that the Uji-Seta forces had not been broken, Kiso no Sakanogami, intending to make his final request for leave, hurried to the Imperial Residence at Rokudō. There, with the Retired Emperor at the forefront, no prayers were offered by the court nobles or high-ranking officials, who said, 'The world is already lost; what can be done?' Though he reached the gate of the Kiso mansion, upon hearing that the forces of the Eastern Provinces had already pressed as far as the riverbank, there was no intention to present his case, so he immediately turned back. Since the lady whom he had first set his heart on at the place called Rokudō-Takakura was there, he went in, intending to bid a final farewell, and would not come out at once. There was a man named Echigo-Chūtai Kōmitsu, who had recently arrived, saying, 'How can you now turn back? Your enemy has already advanced to the riverbank; you would be dying in vain.' Yet since he would not come out, he said, 'If that is so, let us first ride ahead and await you on the mountain of death.' Then, he cut his belly and died. Lord Kiso said, 'Let this be a self-inflicted death to encourage me,' and immediately drew his sword. With the resident of Kōzuke Province, Naba Tarō Hiromasa, as the vanguard, their force numbered no more than about a hundred riders. When they emerged from the gate and looked out toward Rokudō-Kawara, they perceived the forces of the Eastern Provinces, and thirty riders in total had already come forth. Among them, two mounted warriors advanced. One was Shiroya Gorō Tadahiro; the other was Chokushi-Kawara Gōsaburō Arinao. Shiroya said, 'We should wait for the rear guard.' Chokushi-Kawara said, 'If the first line is broken, the remaining troops will be annihilated; just charge!' Then, they clashed and fought. Since Kiso made this day his limit for battle, the forces of the Eastern Provinces advanced with the intent to kill him.

text: 大將軍九郎義經、軍兵共に軍をばせさせ、院御所の覺束なきに、守護し奉らんとて、先づ我身共に直甲五六騎、六條殿へ馳參る。御所には、大膳大夫成忠、御所の東築垣の上に上て、わなゝくわなゝく見まはせば、白旗さと差上、武士ども五六騎のけ甲に戰成て、射向の袖吹靡させ、黒煙蹴立て馳參る。成忠「又木曾が參り候、あなあさまし。」と申ければ、「今度ぞ世の失はて。」とて君も臣も噪がせ給ふ。成忠重て申けるは、「只今馳參る武士ども、笠驗のかはて候、今日始て都へ入る東國の勢と覺候。」と申も果ねば、九郎義經門前へ馳參て馬より下り、門を扣かせ、大音聲を揚て、「東國より前兵衞佐頼朝が舎弟九郎義經こそ參て候へ。明させ給へ。」と申ければ、成忠餘りの嬉しさに、築垣より急ぎ跳りおるゝとて、腰をつき損じたりけれども、痛さは嬉さに紛て覺えず、這々參て、此由奏聞してければ、法皇大に御感在てやがて門を開かせて入られけり。九郎義經其日の裝束には、赤地の錦の直垂に、紫裳濃の鎧著て、鍬形打たる甲の緒しめ、金作の太刀を帶き、切斑の矢負ひ、滋籐の弓の鳥打を紙を廣さ一寸許に切て、左卷にぞ卷たりける。今日の大將軍の驗とぞ見えし。法皇は中門の櫺子より叡覽有て、「ゆゝしげなる者どもかな、皆名乘せよ。」と仰ければ、先づ大將軍九郎義經、次に安田三郎義定、畠山庄司次郎重忠、梶原源太景季、佐々木四郎高綱、澁谷右馬允重資とこそ名乘たれ。義經具して武士は六人鎧は色々也けれども、頬魂事柄何れも劣らず。大膳太夫成忠仰せを承て、九郎義經を大床の際へ召て、合戰の次第を委く御尋あれば、義經畏て申けるは、「義仲が謀叛の事、頼朝大に驚き、範頼義經を始めとして、むねとの兵三十餘人其勢六萬餘騎を參せ候。範頼は勢田より參り候が未參り候はず。義經は宇治の手を責め落いて、先づ此御所守護の爲に馳參じて候。義仲は河原を上りに落候つるを、兵共に追せ候つれば、今は定めて討取候ぬらん。」と、いと事もなげにぞ申されたる。法皇大に御感有て、「神妙也。木曾が餘黨など參て、狼藉もぞ仕る。汝等此御所能々守護せよ。」と仰ければ義經畏り承はて、四方の門を固めて待程に、兵共馳集て、程なく一萬騎許に成にけり。

annotation.translation: The Great General Kyu-ro Yoshitsune, with his army, decided to guard the Imperial Palace, which was in a state of disarray. First, he himself, along with five or six warriors in full armor, galloped to Rokudō-jo. At the palace, Daisai-no-Tayu Naritada climbed atop the eastern earthen wall and, scanning the area with his eyes, saw a white flag raised high. The five or six warriors in armor charged forward, their sleeves billowing as they shot arrows, raising black clouds of dust as they galloped in. Naritada exclaimed, 'Kiso has arrived! How wonderful!' Then both the Emperor and his retainers cried out in joy, 'This is the end of the world!' Naritada then said again, 'The warriors who have just arrived are wearing helmets with lances; they must be the Eastern forces entering the capital for the first time today.' Even after these words were spoken, Yoshitsune rode to the gate, dismounted, and had someone knock on the gate. Raising his voice loudly, he declared, 'From the East comes the younger brother of the Former General of the Eastern Armies, Yorimori's son, Yoshitsune! Open the gate at once!' Overjoyed, Naritada leaped down from the earthen wall, injuring his waist, but the pain was drowned out by his happiness. Crawling forward, he reported the situation to the Emperor. The Emperor was deeply moved and immediately ordered the gate to be opened. Yoshitsune, dressed that day in a red brocade hitatare, wore a dark purple armor, tied the cords of his lacquered kabuto, carried a gold-tasseled sword, bore arrows with cut fletching, and held a bow made of mulberry wood, with a bird-hunting arrowhead cut to about one inch wide, wrapped in his left sleeve. It seemed as if the Great General of the day had finally arrived. From the lattice window of the central gate, the Emperor gazed down and said, 'What magnificent warriors! Introduce yourselves one by one.' First, the Great General Kyu-ro Yoshitsune, followed by Yasuda San-ro Yoshisada, Hatake Sanjiji Jiro Shigetada, Kajiwara Gentai Kagehisa, Sasaki Shiro Takatsuna, and Shibuya Umanosuke Shigezane introduced themselves. Although Yoshitsune and the six warriors were clad in various armors, not a single one of them lacked the spirit of a true warrior. Hearing the Emperor's command, Daisai Daijo Naritada summoned Yoshitsune to the edge of the main dais and inquired in detail about the battle. Yoshitsune, in awe, replied, 'The matter of Yoshinaka's rebellion greatly alarmed Yorimori. Hira no Yoshitsune, along with thirty other warriors, including Yorimori's forces of over sixty thousand cavalry, has come. Hira no Yoshitsune arrived from Setada, but he has not yet arrived. Yoshitsune has driven back the enemy at Uji and has rushed here to guard this Imperial Palace. Yoshinaka, having fallen while ascending the riverbank, has been pursued by the troops; now he is certainly destined to be defeated.' He spoke with such calmness. The Emperor was deeply moved and said, 'This is truly divine! Even the remnants of Kiso's faction have come, bringing chaos. You must guard this Imperial Palace with all your might.' Yoshitsune humbly accepted the command and secured the gates on all four sides. Soon, the troops gathered, and within a short time, they numbered around ten thousand cavalry.

text: 木曾は若しの事あらば、法皇を取參らせて、西國へ落下り、平家と一つに成らんとて、力者廿人汰へて持たりけれども、御所には九郎義經馳參て、守護し奉る由聞えしかば、「さらば」とて、數萬騎の大勢の中へをめいて懸入る。既に討れんとする事度々に及ぶといへども、懸け破り懸け破り通りけり。木曾涙を流て、「かかるべしとだに知たらば、今井を勢田へは遣ざらまし。幼少竹馬の昔より、死ならば一所で死なんとこそ契しに、所々で討れん事こそ悲しけれ。今井が行末を聞かばや。」とて、河原を上りに懸る程に、六條河原と三條河原との間に敵襲て懸れば、取て返し取て返し、僅なる小勢にて、雲霞の如くなる敵の大勢を、五六度までぞ追返す。鴨河さと打渡し粟田口松坂にぞ懸ける。去年信濃を出しには、五萬餘騎と聞えしに今日四宮河原を過るには、主從七騎に成にけり。まして中有の旅の空、思ひやられて哀なり。

annotation.translation: Kiso said, 'If any matter arises, let us take the retired emperor and flee to the western provinces, intending to unite with the Taira clan; although he selected and brought twenty strong men, hearing that Go-Shirakawa had dispatched Yoritomo's son, Go-Hōgen Yoshitsune, to guard the palace, he said, 'Very well,' and charged into the midst of a vast host of tens of thousands of horsemen. Though they were repeatedly attacked, he broke through again and again. Kiso wept, saying, 'Had I even known this would happen, I would not have sent Imai to Seta. From our childhood days as playmates, we had sworn that if death came, we would die together; it is truly sorrowful that we might be slain in separate places. I wonder what Imai's fate is.' As he rode up the riverbank, between Rokujō Riverbank and Sanjō Riverbank, he turned back repeatedly, and with his small force, he drove the enemy, vast as clouds and mist, back five or six times. He crossed the Kamo River, struck across, and charged toward Awadaguchi and Matsuzaka. When he left Shinano last year, it was said there were over fifty thousand horsemen; yet today, as he passes Shigomi Riverbank, his lord and retinue have become only seven riders. Moreover, the empty sky of this journey through the land fills him with sorrowful thoughts.

text: 木曾殿は信濃より、巴、山吹とて、二人の便女を具せられたり。山吹は痛はり有て、都に留りぬ。中にも巴は色白く髮長く、容顏誠に勝れたり。ありがたき強弓、精兵、馬の上、歩立、打物持ては鬼にも神にも逢うと云ふ一人當千の兵也。究竟の荒馬乘り、惡所落し、軍と云へば、實より鎧著せ、大太刀強弓持せて、先づ一方の大將には向けられけり。度々の高名肩を竝ぶる者なし。されば今度も多くの者ども落行討れける中に、七騎が中まで、巴は討れざりけり。

annotation.translation: Lord Ki no was equipped with two female attendants from Shinano, named Tsubone and Yamabuki. Yamabuki was ill and remained in the capital. Among them, Tsubone had fair skin and long hair, and her appearance was truly surpassing. He was a soldier who could not be matched by a thousand, skilled in the difficult use of a powerful bow, expert in handling fine troops, mounted and on foot, wielding striking weapons; it is said that even ghosts and gods would meet him. With ultimate prowess in riding wild horses and making falls from dangerous places, when it came to war, he first put on his armor, carried a large sword and a powerful bow, and then faced the general of one side. There was no one whose high reputation matched his. Therefore, even this time, amidst many falling and being slain, among seven riders, Tsubone was not slain.

text: 木曾は長坂を經て、丹波路へ趣くとも聞えけり。又龍華越に懸て、北國へとも聞えけり。かかりしかとも、「今井が行へを聞ばや。」とて、勢田の方へ落行程に、今井四郎兼平も、八百餘騎で勢田を固めたりけるが僅に五十騎許に打なされ、旗をば卷せて主の覺束なきに、都へとて歸す程に、大津の打出濱にて、木曾殿に行合奉る。互に中一町許より、其と見知て、主從駒を疾めて寄り合たり。木曾殿今井が手を取て宣けるは、「義仲六條河原で如何にも成べかりつれ共、汝が行末の戀しさに、多くの敵の中を懸け破て、是迄は逃たる也。」今井四郎、「御諚誠に忝なう候[1]兼平も勢田で討死仕るべう候つれ共、御行末の覺束なさに、是迄參て候。」とぞ申ける。木曾殿「契は未だ朽せざりけり。義仲が勢は敵に押隔てられ林に馳散て、此邊にもあるらんぞ。汝が卷せて持せたる旗上させよ。」と宣へば、今井が旗を差し上たり。京より落る勢ともなく、勢田より落る者ともなく、今井が旗を見附けて、三百餘騎ぞ馳集る。木曾殿大に悦で「此勢あらば、などか最後の軍せざるべき。爰にしぐらうて見ゆるは、誰が手やらん。」「甲斐の一條次郎殿とこそ承候へ。」「勢は幾等程有やらん」「六千餘騎とこそ聞え候ヘ。」「さらばよい敵ごさんなれ。同う死なば、よからう敵に懸合て大勢の中でこそ討死をもせめ。」とて眞先にこそ進みけれ。

annotation.translation: It was heard that Kiso was going through Nagasaka to the Tanba Road, and also that he was crossing Ryugao to go to the Northern Provinces. However, when it was said, 'Let us go to Iwai,' he turned toward the Seta direction. While the plan was to retreat to Seta, Iwai no Shiro Kanehira had also fortified Seta with over eight hundred cavalrymen, but they were reduced to barely fifty riders, rolled up their banners, and, seeing their lord in a state of confusion, were returning to the capital. At Otsu's Uchide-hama, they met Lord Kiso. From about a distance of one town, they recognized each other and hurried their horses to meet. Lord Kiso took Iwai's hand and said, 'Although Yoshinaka surely met his end at Rokujō Kawara, out of longing for your fate, I broke through many enemies and have come this far.' Iwai no Shiro replied, 'Your command is truly an honor. Although I should have died in battle at Seta, out of concern for your state, I have come this far.' Lord Kiso said, 'The oath has not yet rotted. Yoshinaka's forces, pressed by the enemy, scattered into the woods; perhaps some remain in this area. Raise the banner you have rolled up and are carrying.' Iwai raised his banner. Without any troops retreating from the capital or from Seta, seeing Iwai's banner, over three hundred riders gathered and galloped to join him. Lord Kiso, greatly pleased, said, 'If we have such forces, why should we not fight a final battle? Who is it that stands here, looking like this?' 'It is Lord Ichijō Jirō of Kai,' he was told. 'How many troops do you have?' 'It is said there are over six thousand.' 'Then, let us face the enemy with joy. If we must die together, it is better to charge into the enemy ranks and die in the midst of a great force.' With these words, he advanced first.

text: 木曾左馬頭其日の裝束には、赤地の錦の直垂に、唐綾威の鎧著て、鍬形打たる甲の緒しめ、いか物作の大太刀帶き、石打の矢の、其日の軍に射て、少々殘たるを、首高に負なし、滋籐の弓持て、聞る木曾の鬼葦毛と云ふ馬の究て太う逞に金覆輪の鞍置て乘たりける。鐙蹈張立上り、大音聲を揚て名乘けるは、「日比は聞けん物を、木曾冠者。今は見るらん、左馬頭兼伊豫守朝日將軍源義仲ぞや。甲斐の一條次郎とこそきけ。互に好い敵ぞ。義仲討て兵衞佐に見せよや。」とて喚いて懸く。一條次郎、「唯今名乘は、大將軍ぞ。餘すな、洩すな、若黨、討や。」とて大勢の中に取籠て、我討取んとぞ進ける。木曾三百餘騎、六千餘騎が中を堅ざま横ざま蜘蛛手十文字に懸破て、後へつと出たれば、五十騎許に成にけり。そこを破て行く程に、土肥次郎實平、二千餘騎で支たり。そこをも破て行く程に、あそこでは四五百騎、こゝでは二三百騎、百四五十騎、百騎ばかりが中を、懸け破り々々行く程に、主從五騎にぞ成にける。五騎が中迄、巴は討れざりけり。木曾殿「おのれは、とう／＼、女なれば、何地へも落ゆけ。義仲は討死せんと思ふ也。若し人手に懸らば、自害をせんずれば、木曾殿の最後の軍に、女を具せられたりけりなど言れん事も、然るべからず。」と宣ひけれども、猶落も行ざりけるが、餘りに言はれ奉て、「あはれ好らう敵がな。最後の軍して見せ奉らん。」とて、引へたる處に武藏國に聞えたる大力、御田八郎師重、三十騎許で出來たり。巴其中へ懸入、御田八郎に押ならべ、むずと取て引き落し、我が乘たる鞍の前輪に押つけて、ちとも働かさず頸ねぢ切て捨てけり。其後物具脱棄て、東國の方へ落ぞ行く。手塚太郎討死す。手塚の別當落にけり。

annotation.translation: On that day, Kiso no Saba no Kami wore a crimson brocade hitatare and a Tang-style lacquered armor with a helmet secured with cords, and carried a great sword of unusual craftsmanship. He took the few remaining arrowheads of his stone-piercing arrows and shot them in that day's battle, then carried the heads high on his shoulders. He held a cypress bow, mounted the horse named Kiso no Oni Ashigara, which was described as incredibly large and powerful, with a gold-rimmed saddle, and rode forth. His stirrups were raised and his feet planted firmly, raising a great sound as he called out, 'Today, you may hear of me, Kiso no Gongen. Now you shall see me, Saba no Kami, also known as Iyo no Kami, the Asahi General, Minamoto no Yoshinaka. It is said that I am the one and only Jirō of Kai. We are worthy enemies. Strike down Yoshinaka and show him to the War Minister.' And so he shouted and charged. Jirō of the Ichijō line replied, 'That voice I just heard belongs to the Great General. Do not delay, do not let it slip, my young warriors, strike him down!' And so, amidst the great throng, he broke through, intending to defeat him. The three hundred and more of Kiso's cavalry, amidst six thousand or more, broke through in solid and horizontal formations, like a spider's web in a cross pattern, and rushed out to the rear, reducing their numbers to about fifty riders. As they broke through further, Tōi no Jirō Saneyoshi came with over two thousand riders. Breaking through that line as well, they encountered four or five hundred riders over there, two or three hundred here, one hundred and forty to fifty, and about a hundred, breaking through them one after another until they were reduced to five riders, including their lord and vassal. Even amidst these five, Tomoe was not struck down. Lord Kiso said, 'You are, indeed, a woman. Wherever you go, you will fall. I think Yoshinaka will die in battle. If we fall into enemy hands, and I do not commit suicide, it will be said that among Lord Kiso's final battle, a woman was included, which would be unacceptable.' Although he spoke thus, she still did not retreat, but was urged so greatly that she said, 'Ah, what a fine enemy! Let us make a final stand and show them!' annotation.summary: On that day, Kiso no Saba no Kami wore a crimson brocade hitatare and a Tang-style lacquered armor with a helmet secured with cords, and carried a great sword of unusual craftsmanship. He took the few remaining arrowheads of his stone-piercing arrows and shot them in that day's battle, then carried the heads high on his shoulders. He held a cypress bow, mounted the horse named Kiso no Oni Ashigara, which was described as incredibly large and powerful, with a gold-rimmed saddle, and rode forth. His stirrups were raised and his feet planted firmly, raising a great sound as he called out, 'Today, you may hear of me, Kiso no Gongen. Now you shall see me, Saba no Kami, also known as Iyo no Kami, the Asahi General, Minamoto no Yoshinaka. It is said that I am the one and only Jirō of Kai. We are worthy enemies. Strike down Yoshinaka and show him to the War Minister.' And so he shouted and charged. Jirō of the Ichijō line replied, 'That voice I just heard belongs to the Great General. Do not delay, do not let it slip, my young warriors, strike him down!' And so, amidst the great throng, he broke through, intending to defeat him. The three hundred and more of Kiso's cavalry, amidst six thousand or more, broke through in solid and horizontal formations, like a spider's web in a cross pattern, and rushed out to the rear, reducing their numbers to about fifty riders. text: 今井四郎、木曾殿、主從二騎に成て宣けるは、「日來は何とも覺えぬ鎧が、今日は重う成たるぞや。」今井四郎申けるは、「御身も未疲れさせ給はず、御馬も弱り候はず。何に依てか一領の御著背長を重うは思食候べき。其は御方に御勢が候はねば、臆病でこそ、さは思召候へ。兼平一人候とも、餘の武者千騎と思召せ。矢七八候へば、暫く防ぎ矢仕らん。あれに見え候は、粟津の松原と申。あの松の中で、御自害候へ。」とて、打て行く程に、又荒手の武者五十騎許出來たり。「君はあの松原へ入せ給へ。兼平は此敵防ぎ候はん。」と申ければ、木曾殿のたまひけるは「義仲都にて如何にも成べかりつるが、是迄逃れ來るは汝と一所で死なんと思ふ爲也。所々で討れんより一所でこそ討死をもせめ。」とて、馬の鼻を竝て、懸んとし給へば、今井四郎馬より飛下、主の馬の口に取附て申けるは「弓矢取りは、年比日比如何なる高名候へども、最後の時不覺しつれば、永き瑕にて候也。御身は疲させ給ひて候。續く勢は候はず。敵に押隔てられ、いふかひなき人の郎等に組落されさせ給て討れさせ給なば、さばかり日本國に聞えさせ給ひつる木曾殿をば、何某が郎等の討奉たるなど申さん事こそ口惜う候へ。唯あの松原へ入せ給へ。」と申ければ、木曾「さらば」とて、粟津の松原へぞ駈け給ふ。

annotation.translation: Imai Shiro and the Lord Kiso, now two riders on horseback, declared: "Though I felt no heaviness in my armor these past days, today it has become heavy." Imai Shiro said: "Your Lordship has not yet grown weary, nor has your horse grown weak. Why should you think a single suit of armor has become heavy? This is because you have no reinforcements with you; it is out of cowardice that you feel this way. Even if only Kenpei is here, think of him as a thousand warriors. When they shoot seven or eight arrows, I will hold them off for a while. What you see ahead is the pine grove of Awazu. There, in the midst of those pines, commit suicide." As they rode on, about fifty warriors from the rough ranks appeared. "Enter that pine grove, my Lord," he said, "and Kenpei shall hold off these enemies." Lord Kiso replied: "I had intended to meet my fate in the capital, but the reason I have fled thus far is that I wished to die with you. Rather than being defeated in various places, let us die together." Then, aligning their horses' heads, he was about to charge, when Imai Shiro leaped from his horse, seized the bridle of his master's horse, and said: "Even if archers are as renowned as they may be today, if they do not act with awareness in the final moments, it will be an eternal stain. Your Lordship is weary, and there are no further reinforcements. If you are pushed back by the enemy and captured by the retainers of those without honor, and killed by them, then who will say that Lord Kiso, whose fame has spread throughout Japan, was killed by the retainers of some insignificant person? That would be truly regrettable. Only enter that pine grove." Hearing this, Lord Kiso said, "Very well," and spurred his horse toward the pine grove of Awazu.

text: 今井四郎唯一騎、五十騎許が中へかけ入り、鐙蹈張立上り、大音聲揚て、名乘けるは、「日比は音にも聞きつらん、今は目にも見給へ。木曾殿の乳母子今井の四郎兼平、生年三十三に罷成る。さる者ありとは、鎌倉殿までも知召されたるらんぞ。兼平討て、見參に入よ。」とて、射殘たる八筋の矢を、指つめ引詰散々に射る。死生は知らず、矢庭に敵八騎射落す。其後打物ぬいであれに馳あひ、是に馳合ひ、切て回るに、面を合する者ぞなき。分捕餘たしたりけり。「唯射取や。」とて、中に取籠め雨の降樣に射けれども、鎧好れば裏かゝず、明間を射ねば手も負はず。

annotation.translation: Imai no Shiro, riding alone, charged into the midst of about fifty horsemen, raised his stirrups, stood upright, and raised a great voice, declaring: 'You may have heard of my name in sound before; now see me with your own eyes. I am Imai no Shiro Kanehira, the wet nurse and foster son of Lord Ki no Tono. I have just completed my thirty-third year. Even the Lord of Kamakura must have heard that such a man exists. Strike down Kanehira and come to pay your respects!' Thus, he drew the remaining eight arrows from his quiver, nocked them, and loosed them in wild volleys. Whether he lived or died he knew not; in the midst of the arrows, he shot down eight enemy horsemen. After that, he rushed to meet the charging troops, drew near, and engaged in close combat, yet there was no one whose face he struck. He had captured many. 'Let us only shoot them down!' they cried, and surrounded him, raining arrows upon him like rain; but his armor was so well made that the arrows did not penetrate, and because they did not shoot through the gaps, they did not wound his hands.

text: 木曾殿は唯一騎、粟津の松原へ駈給ふが、正月廿一日、入相許の事なるに、薄氷は張たりけり。深田有とも知らずして、馬を颯とうち入たれば、馬のかしらも見えざりけり。あふれども／＼、打ども／＼動かず。今井が行末の覺束なさに、振あふぎ給へる内甲を、三浦の石田次郎爲久追懸て、よ引てひやうと射る。痛手なれば、まかふを馬の首に當て俯し給へる處に、石田が郎等二人落合て、終に木曾殿の頸をとてけり。太刀の鋒に貫ぬき、高く指上げ、大音聲を揚て、「此日比日本國に聞えさせ給ひつる木曾殿をば、三浦石田次郎爲久が討奉たるぞや。」と名のりければ、今井四郎軍しけるが、是を聞き、「今は誰をかばはむとて軍をもすべき。是を見給へ、東國の殿原、日本一の剛の者の自害する手本。」とて、太刀の鋒を口に含み、馬より倒に飛落ち、貫かてぞ失にける。去てこそ粟津の軍は無りけれ。

annotation.translation: Lord Kiso, riding alone, galloped to the pine grove of Awazu, but on the twenty-first day of the first month, he had arrived at the time of the battle, and the thin ice had already formed. Unaware of the deep fields, he drove his horse into them, and not even the horse's head could be seen. He struggled and struggled, but could not move. Seeing the weakness of Imai's movements, Miura no Ishida Jiro Tadamasa pursued and shot at him with a bow drawn. Since the wound was painful, Lord Kiso lowered his helmet over his horse's head and bowed his head; then two of Ishida's retainers joined him, and finally they struck at Lord Kiso's neck. Pierced by the tip of the sword, he raised his head high, raised his voice loudly, and declared, "Today, the Lord Kiso, whose fame has spread throughout Japan, has been defeated by Miura Ishida Jiro Tadamasa." Hearing this, Imai Shiro, who had been charging, said, "Now, whom shall I protect by charging? Look at this! The field of the Eastern lords, the model of a self-sacrifice by the strongest man in Japan." Saying this, he placed the tip of his sword in his mouth, fell headlong from his horse, and died pierced. Thus the battle of Awazu came to an end.

text: 今井が兄樋口次郎兼光は、十郎藏人討んとて、河内國長野城へ越たりけるが、其にては討漏しぬ。紀伊國名草に有りと聞えしかば、やがて續いて越たりけるが、都に軍有りと聞て、馳上る。淀の大渡の橋で、今井が下人行合たり。「あな心憂、是は何地へとて渡せ給ひ候ぞ。君は討れさせ給ぬ。今井殿は自害。」と申ければ、樋口次郎涙をはら／＼と流いて、「是聞給へ、殿原、君に御志思ひ參せ給はん人人は、是より何地へも落行き、出家入道して、乞食頭陀の行をも立て、後世をも弔參せ給へ。兼光は都へ上り討死して、冥途にて君の見參に入、今井四郎を今一度見んと思ふぞ。」と云ければ、五百餘騎の勢あそこに引へ、こゝに引へ、落ゆく程に、鳥羽の南の門を出けるには、其勢僅に廿餘騎にぞ成にける。樋口次郎今日既に都へ入と聞えしかば、黨も高家も、七條、朱雀、四塚さまへ馳向ふ。樋口が手に、茅野太郎と云ふ者有り。四塚に幾も馳向うたる敵の中へ馳入り、大音聲を揚て、「此御中に甲斐の一條次郎殿の御手の人やまします。」と問ければ、「強一條次郎殿の手で、軍をばするか、誰にも合へかし。」とて、どと笑ふ。笑はれて名のりけるは、「かう申す者は信濃國諏訪上宮の住人、茅野大夫光家が子に、茅野太郎光廣、必ず一條の次郎殿の御手を尋るには非ず、弟の茅野七郎それにあり。光廣が子共二人信濃國に候が、あはれ我父は、好てや死にたるらん。惡てや死にたるらんと歎かん處に、弟の七郎が前で討死して、子共にたしかに聞せんと思ふ爲也。敵をば嫌まじ。」とて、あれに馳合ひ、これに馳合ひ、敵三騎きて落し、四人に當る敵に押雙べ引組でどうと落ち刺違てぞ死にける。

annotation.translation: Imai's older brother, Higuchi Jiro Kanehikari, went to Kachino Castle in Kachino Province to try to kill the tenth son of the Chamberlain, but failed to do so. Upon hearing that he was in Natsuki, Kii Province, he immediately crossed over there, but hearing that an army was in the capital, he hurried back. At the bridge of Ohashi in Yodo, he met Imai's retainer. 'Alas, how sorrowful! Where are you crossing to, my lord? You are being slain. Lord Imai has committed suicide.' When he said this, Higuchi Jiro wept in torrents: 'Hear me, my lord. Those who have thought of serving you from now on will scatter to every place, become monks or priests, set out on the path of begging and asceticism, and mourn the future. Kanehikari will ascend to the capital and die in battle, enter the path of the dead, and see you again, so that I may see Imai Shiro once more.' When he said this, the force of over five hundred cavalry was drawn there, drawn here; as they began to fall back, when they exited the southern gate of southern Toba, their force had dwindled to only about twenty cavalry. Since it was heard that Higuchi had already entered the capital, his faction and the high-ranking officials galloped toward Shijo, Suzaku, and Yotsuka. Among Higuchi's men was a man named Chono Taro. He charged into the midst of the enemies who had galloped toward Yotsuka, raised his voice loudly, and asked, 'Is the person in the armor of Lord Ichijo Jiro of Kai Province among you?' They replied, 'If it is the hand of the strong Lord Ichijo Jiro, who will not oppose the army?' and laughed loudly. The one who was laughed at and identified himself said, 'The one who says this is Chono Dairo Mitsuhiro, son of Chono Dairo Mitsuie, a resident of Kamimiya, Suwa Province in Shinano Province. If you are seeking the hand of Lord Ichijo Jiro, it is not me but my younger brother, Chono Shichiro. My two children are in Shinano Province. Alas, how would my father have died? Would he have died in a good way or a bad way? He would lament at the place where his younger brother Shichiro died in battle, so that his children would certainly hear of it. He would not hate the enemy.' With these words, he galloped here, galloped there, struck down three enemy cavalry, and when four enemies attacked him, he was pushed back, locked in a struggle, fell with a loud crash, and died by a different sword thrust.

text: 樋口次郎は兒玉黨に結ほれたりければ、兒玉の人ども寄合て、「弓矢取習ひ我も人も廣い中へ入らんとするは、自然の事の在ん時の一まとの息をも休め、暫しの命をも續んと思ふ爲也。されば樋口次郎が我等にむすぼほれけんも、さこそは思ひけめ。今度の我等が勳功には樋口が命を申請ん。」とて使者を立てゝ、「日比は木曾殿の御内に、今井、樋口とて聞え給しかども、今は木曾殿討れさせ給ひぬ。何か苦かるべき、我等が中へ降人に成給へ。勳功の賞に申かへて命ばかり助奉らん。出家入道をもして後世を弔ひ參せ給へ。」と云ければ、樋口次郎聞ゆる兵なれども、運や盡にけん、兒玉黨の中へ降人にこそ成にけれ。是を九郎御曹司に申す。御所へ奏聞して宥められたりしを傍の公卿殿上人、局の女房達、「木曾が法住寺殿へ寄せて、鬨を作り君をも惱し參らせ、火をかけて、多の人々を滅し失ひしには、あそこにもこゝにも、今井樋口といふ聲のみこそ有しか。これらを宥められんは口惜かるべし。」と、面々に申されければ、又死罪に定めらる。

annotation.translation: Since Higurōji was allied with the Kodama party, the members of the Kodama gathered and said, "To practice archery and enter the broad field, whether one is oneself or another, is a natural matter; one should not even rest a single breath in such a moment, nor should one think to prolong even a brief life. Therefore, Higurōji must have thought that he was joining us. In this our current merit, we shall petition for Higurō's life." Thus they sent an envoy, saying, "It was reported to Lord Kiso that there were men named Imai and Higurō, but now Lord Kiso has been killed. If you are in any distress, become a surrenderer among us. In the reward for our merit, we shall petition to spare only your life. You may even become a monk and pray for the afterlife." When Higurō heard this, though he was a warrior, his luck had come to an end, and he became a surrenderer among the Kodama party. This was reported to Kyūgō no Go-shōji. After the Imperial Court had heard the report and pardoned him, the nearby court nobles and the ladies of the palace said, "When Kiso went to Hokoji Temple, raised the war cry, troubled the Emperor, set fire, and destroyed many people, all that remained were the names 'Imai' and 'Higurō' here and there. To pardon these men is indeed regrettable." Thus, by the words of each of them, he was again sentenced to death.

text: 同二十二日、新攝政殿とどめられ給ひ、本の攝政還著し給ふ。僅六十日の内に替られ給へば、未だ見果ぬ夢の如し。昔粟田の關白は、悦申の後唯七箇日だにこそおはせしか。是は六十日とは云へども、其間に節會も除目も行はれしかば、思出なきにもあらず。

annotation.translation: On the same twenty-second day, he was detained in the new Regent's palace, and the original Regent returned to his post. For he was replaced within just sixty days, it is like a dream that has not yet been fulfilled. In the past, the Kampaku of Awata was present for only seven days after receiving joy. Although this is said to be sixty days, since festivals and appointments took place during that time, it is not without memory.

text: 同廿四日、木曾左馬頭、幵餘黨五人が頸、大路を渡さる。樋口次郎は降人なりしが、頻に頸の伴せんと申ければ、藍摺の水干立烏帽子で渡されけり。同廿五日、樋口次郎終に斬られぬ。範頼義經樣々に申されけれども、「今井、樋口、楯、根井とて、木曾が四天王の其一つ也。是等を宥められんは、養虎の愁有るべし。」と、殊に沙汰有て斬られけるとぞ聞えし。傳に聞く、虎狼の國衰て諸侯蜂の如く起し時、はい公先に咸陽宮へ入と云へども、項羽が後に來らん事を恐て、妻は美人をも犯かさず、金銀珠玉をも掠めず、徒に凾谷の關を守て、漸漸に敵を滅して天下を治する事を得たりき。されば木曾左馬頭、先都へ入といふとも、頼朝朝臣の命に從がはましかば、彼はい公が謀には劣らざらまし。

annotation.translation: On the same twenty-fourth day, Kiso no Samanokami had the heads of the remaining five ringleaders cut off and sent them across the main road. Higuchi no Jirō, who was a surrendered man, had repeatedly pleaded to be allowed to accompany the heads, and so he was sent across wearing an indigo-dyed cotton robe and a black lacquered hat. On the same twenty-fifth day, Higuchi no Jirō was finally not executed. Although Yoritomo and Yoshitsune urged him in various ways, it was reported that he was specifically ordered to be executed, saying, 'Imai, Higuchi, Tate, and Ne are the Four Heavenly Kings of Kiso, one of them. If these men were pardoned, it would be like nurturing a tiger and inviting trouble.' According to the chronicles, when the nation of tigers and wolves declined and the feudal lords rose up like bees, even though the Duke of Han was said to have entered Xianyang Palace first, fearing that Xiang Yu would come later, he did not violate any of his beautiful wives, did not plunder gold, silver, pearls, or jade, but merely guarded the Hangu Pass, gradually destroyed the enemy, and was able to bring order to the world. Therefore, even though Kiso no Samanokami was said to have entered the capital first, if he had obeyed the command of Lord Taira no Yoritomo, he would not have fallen short of the Duke of Han's strategy.

text: 平家は去年の冬の比より、讃岐國八島磯を出て、攝津國難波潟へ押渡り、福原の舊都に居住して、西は一谷を城郭に構へ、東は生田森を大手の木戸口とぞ定めける。其内、福原、兵庫、板宿、須磨に籠る勢、是は山陽道八箇國、南海道六箇國、都合十四箇國を打隨へて、召るゝ所の軍兵也。十萬餘騎とぞ聞えし。一谷は北は山、南は海、口は狹くて奧廣し。岸高くして屏風を立たるに異ならず。北の山際より、南の海の遠淺迄、大石を重上げ、大木を伐て逆茂木にひき、深き所には大船どもをそばだてて掻楯にかき、城の面の高櫓には、一人當千と聞ゆる四國鎭西の兵ども甲冑弓箭を帶して、雲霞の如くになみ居たり。やぐらの下には、鞍置馬共、十重廿重に引立てたり。常に大皷を打て亂聲を爲す。一張の弓の勢は、半月胸の前に懸り、三尺の劍の光は、秋の霜腰の間に横へたり。高き所には赤旗多く打立たれば、春風に吹れて天に翻るは、火焔の燃上るに異ならず。

annotation.translation: The Heike, since last winter, having departed from Yashima Island in Sanuki Province and crossed over to Naniwagata in Settsu Province, took up residence in the former capital of Fukuhara; on the west they constructed Ichinotani into a castle, and on the east they designated Ikuta Mori as the main gate, so it is said. Within this, the forces stationed in Fukuhara, Hyogo, Itabuku, and Suma are the soldiers summoned from the eight provinces of the San'yō region and the six provinces of the Nankai region, totaling fourteen provinces. It is said that they numbered over ten thousand cavalry. Ichinotani has mountains to the north and the sea to the south; the entrance is narrow while the interior is vast. The shore is high, resembling a standing screen. From the northern mountain edge to the shallow southern sea, large stones are piled high, large trees are felled and drawn as palisades, and in deep places, large ships are set up as oar-shields. On the high towers of the castle's face, the soldiers of the four nations of Satsuma and Saishū, famed as one man worth a thousand, stand clad in armor and carrying bows and arrows, like clouds and mist. Beneath the towers, saddled horses are drawn up in ten and twenty layers. Great drums are constantly beaten, creating a chaotic sound. The power of a single bow is such that a half-moon hangs before the chest; the light of a three-shaku sword lies across the waist like autumn frost. Where the high places are, many red flags are raised, and when blown by the spring wind, they turn in the sky, not unlike flames burning upward.

text: 平家福原へ渡給ひて後は、四國の兵ども隨ひ奉らず。中にも阿波讃岐の在廳ども、平家を背いて、源氏に付むとしけるが、「抑我等は昨日今日まで、平家に隨うたるものの、今日始めて源氏の方へ参りたりとも、よも用ゐられじ。いざや平家に矢一つ射懸て、其を面にして參らん。」とて、門脇中納言、子息越前三位、能登守父子三人、備前國下津井にましますと聞えしかば討たてまつらんとて、兵船十餘艘で寄せたりける。能登守是を聞き、「惡い奴原かな。昨日今日迄、我等が馬の草切たる奴原が、既に契りを變ずるにこそ有なれ。其儀ならば、一人も洩さず討てや。」とて、小船共に取乘て、「餘すな、漏すな。」とて攻め給へば、四國の兵共、人目ばかりに矢一つ射て、退んとこそ思ひけるに、手痛う攻られ奉て、叶はじとや思ひけん、遠負にして引退き、都の方へ逃上るが、淡路國福良の泊に著にけり。其國に源氏二人有り、故六條判官爲義が末子、賀茂冠者義嗣、淡路冠者義久と聞えしを、西國の兵共大將に憑んで、城廓を構へて待處に、能登殿やがて押寄攻給へば、一日戰ひ賀茂冠者討死す。淡路冠者は痛手負て、自害してけり。能登殿、防ぎ矢射ける兵ども、百三十餘人が頸切て、討手の交名記いて、福原へ參らせらる。

annotation.translation: After the Taira had crossed to Fukuhara, the soldiers of Shikoku did not follow them. Among them, the officials of Awa and Sanuki, turning their backs on the Taira, were inclined to join the Minamoto, thinking, "In truth, until yesterday and today we have been following the Taira; even if we were to go to the Minamoto side for the first time today, we would surely not be employed. Come, let us shoot one arrow at the Taira, display it as proof, and go to them." Hearing that the Gate Companion Chūnagon and his son, the Third Rank of Kōsuke, and the Governor of Noto, the three of them father and son, were at Shōtsu in Bizen Province, they decided to attack and dispatched more than ten warships. The Governor of Noto, hearing this, said, "Wretched creatures! Those very same wretches who, until yesterday and today, have cut the grass for our horses, now to change their oath! If that is the case, kill them all without letting one escape." Then, boarding small boats together, shouting, "Leave none, let none escape!" they attacked fiercely. The soldiers of Shikoku, thinking only of shooting one arrow to repel them and retreat, were struck with painful force; wondering if they could possibly hold out, they withdrew over a distance and fled toward the capital, landing at the harbor of Fukura in Awaji Province. In that province were two Minamoto: the youngest son of the late Sixth Court Councilor Tameyoshi, known as the Kamogawa Koroshi Yoshitsugu, and the Awaji Kamogawa Yoshitsugu. Hearing this, the soldiers of the Western Provinces, relying on their general, built a castle and waited in position. When the Lord of Noto soon pressed the attack, they fought for one day, and the Kamogawa Koroshi fell in battle. The Awaji Kamogawa, having suffered a grievous wound, committed suicide. The Lord of Noto had the necks cut from the soldiers who had shot the defensive arrows, one hundred and thirty in number, their names as attackers were recorded, and they were sent to Fukuhara.

text: 門脇中納言其より福原へ上り給ふ。子息達は伊豫の河野四郎召せども參らぬを責んとて、四國へぞ渡られける。先づ兄の越前三位通盛卿、阿波國花園城に著給ふ。弟能登守、讃岐の八島へ渡り給ふと聞えしかば、河野四郎通信は、安藝國の住人沼田次郎は母方の伯父[2]なりけりば、一つに成んとて、安藝國へ推渡る。能登守是を聞き、やがて讃岐の八島を出でて追はれけるが、既に備後國蓑島に懸て、次の日沼田城へ寄せ給ふ。沼田次郎、河野四郎一つに成て、防ぎ戰ふ。能登殿やがて押寄て攻給へば、一日一夜ふせぎ戰ひ沼田次郎叶はじとや思ひけん、甲を脱いで、降人に參る。河野四郎は猶從ひ奉らず、其勢五百餘騎有けるが、僅に五十騎許に討成れ、城を出て行く程に、能登殿の侍、平八兵衞爲員二百騎許が中に取籠られて主從七騎に討成れ、助け船に乘んと、細道に懸て渚の方へ落行程に、平八兵衞が子息、讃岐七郎義範、究竟の弓の上手ではあり、追懸て七騎を矢庭に五騎射落す。河野四郎只主從二騎になりにけり。河野が身に替へて思ひける郎等を讃岐七郎押竝べて組で落ち、取て押て頸を掻んとする所に、河野四郎取て返し、郎等が上なる讃岐七郎が頸掻切て深田へ投入、大音聲を揚て、「河野四郎越智通信、生年廿一、かうこそ軍をばすれ。我と思はん人々は留よや。」とて、郎等を肩に引懸け、そこをつと迯て小舟に乘り、伊豫國へぞ渡りける。能登殿河野をも打漏されたれども、沼田次郎が降人たるを召具して、福原へぞ參られける。

annotation.translation: The Chancellor of the Left, Kadokawa, departed for Fuhara. He blamed the sons of Kono no Shiro in Iyo, who had summoned them but did not come, and thus they crossed to Shikoku. First, the elder brother, the Third Rank of Echizen, Katsunori, went to Hanazono Castle in Awa. When it was heard that the younger brother, the Governor of Noto, had crossed to Yashima in Sanuki, Kono no Shiro Tsunemasa, whose mother's uncle was Numata no Jiro of Awa Province, decided to unite with them and crossed to Awa Province. Noto no Mori heard of this and immediately left Yashima in Sanuki to pursue, but Numata no Jiro had already set up camp at Mimajima in Bingo Province and the next day approached Numata Castle. Numata no Jiro and Kono no Shiro united and defended and fought. Noto no Mori immediately attacked and assaulted them; after defending and fighting for one day and one night, Numata no Jiro, thinking he could not prevail, removed his armor and became a captive. Kono no Shiro, however, still did not accept him; though his force numbered over five hundred horsemen, they were reduced to barely fifty, and as they were leaving the castle, the retainers of Noto no Mori, Hachibei Tsuyoshi, were trapped among about two hundred horsemen, and their lord and seven retainers were killed. Hoping to escape by boat, they took a narrow path and headed toward the shore, but Hachibei's son, Sanuki no Shiro Yoshinori, who was a master of archery, pursued and shot down five of the seven horsemen in the midst of battle. Kono no Shiro was left with only himself and two retainers. The retainers of Kono no Shiro, whom he had taken in his stead, were pushed back by Sanuki no Shiro and were about to be seized and have their necks cut when Kono no Shiro turned and, cutting off the head of Sanuki no Shiro who was above the retainers, threw it into a deep field, raised a loud voice, and said, "Kono no Shiro, Chikazane of Ochi, twenty-one years old; thus shall the army be! Those who think of me, stay!" Then he threw the retainers over his shoulders, fled, boarded a small boat, and crossed to Iyo Province. Although Noto no Mori had let Kono no Shiro escape, he summoned Numata no Jiro, who had become a captive, and departed for Fuhara.

text: 又淡路國の住人安摩六郎忠景、平家を背いて、源氏に心を通しけるが、大船二艘に兵粮米物具、積で都の方へ上る程に、能登殿福原にて、これをきゝ、小舟十艘計おし浮べて追はれけり。安摩六郎、西宮の沖にて返し合せて防戰ふ。手痛う責められ奉て、叶はじとや思ひけん、引退て和泉國吹飯浦に著にけり。紀伊國の住人園邊兵衞忠康、これも平家を背いて源氏につかんとしけるが、安摩六郎が能登殿に攻られ奉て、吹飯に有と聞えしかば、其勢百騎計で馳來て一つになる。能登殿やがて續いて攻給へば、一日一夜防ぎ戰ひ、安摩六郎、園邊兵衞、叶はじとや思ひけん、家子郎等に防矢射させ、身がらは迯て京へ上る。能登殿防矢射ける兵ども、二百餘人が頸切りかけて、福原へこそ參られけれ。又伊豫國の住人河野四郎通信、豐後國の住人臼杵次郎惟高、緒方三郎惟義、同心して都合其勢二千餘人、備前國へ押渡り、今木城にぞ籠ける。能登守是を聞き、福原より三千餘騎で馳下り、今木城を攻め給ふ。能登殿「彼奴原はこはい御敵で候。重て勢を給はらん。」と申されければ、福原より數萬騎の大勢を向らるゝ由聞えし程に、城の内の兵ども、手のきは戰ひ、分捕高名し究て、「平家は大勢でまします也。我等は無勢也。如何にも叶まじ。こゝをば落て、暫く息を續がん。」とて、臼杵次郎、緒方三郎舟に取り乘り、鎭西へ押し渡る。河野は伊豫へぞ渡りける。能登殿「今は討つべき敵なし。」とて、福原へこそ參られけれ。大臣殿を始め奉て平家一門の公卿殿上人寄合ひて、能登殿毎度の高名をぞ一同に感じ合れける。

annotation.translation: Furthermore, Yasumasa Rokuro Tadayoshi, a resident of Awaji Province, having turned his back on the Taira and opened his heart to the Minamoto, while loading two large boats with provisions, equipment, and rice, preparing to ascend to the capital, was learned of this by Lord Tono at Fukuhara; he then launched approximately ten small boats to pursue them. Yasumasa Rokuro, at the offing of Nishinomiya, turned to engage in battle. Pressed hard by a painful attack, thinking that success would not be possible, he withdrew and settled in Fukuiura, Izumi Province. Sonabe Hebei Tadayasu, a resident of Kii Province, also attempted to turn his back on the Taira and serve the Minamoto; however, when he heard that Yasumasa Rokuro had been attacked by Lord Tono and had taken refuge in Fukui, he gathered a force of approximately one hundred horsemen and joined forces with him. As Lord Tono immediately followed up with an attack, they defended for a day and a night. Yasumasa Rokuro and Sonabe Hebei, thinking that success would not be possible, ordered their retainers to shoot defense arrows while they themselves escaped to the capital. The soldiers of Lord Tono who had been shooting defense arrows, over two hundred of them, were beheaded, and only then were they allowed to return to Fukuhara. Furthermore, Kono Shiro Tsunamichi, a resident of Iyo Province; Usuki Jiro Tadahiro, a resident of Bungo Province; and Ogata Saburo Tadayoshi, acting in concert, gathered a force of approximately two thousand and crossed to Bizen Province, taking refuge in Imaki Castle. Lord Tono heard of this and, with over three thousand horsemen, descended from Fukuhara to attack Imaki Castle. Lord Tono said, 'Those rogues are truly formidable enemies; I shall now send a heavier force.' As word spread that a great army of tens of thousands of horsemen was being dispatched from Fukuhara, the soldiers within the castle fought to the utmost, taking many spoils, and finally concluded, 'The Taira are numerous and mighty; we are few. There is no way we can prevail. Let us abandon this place and temporarily draw breath.' Thus, Usuki Jiro and Ogata Saburo boarded their boats and pushed across to Chikuzen. Kono crossed to Iyo. Lord Tono then said, 'Now there is no enemy left to attack,' and returned to Fukuhara. annotation.summary: Furthermore, Yasumasa Rokuro Tadayoshi, a resident of Awaji Province, having turned his back on the Taira and opened his heart to the Minamoto, while loading two large boats with provisions, equipment, and rice, preparing to ascend to the capital, was learned of this by Lord Tono at Fukuhara; he then launched approximately ten small boats to pursue them. Yasumasa Rokuro, at the offing of Nishinomiya, turned to engage in battle. Pressed hard by a painful attack, thinking that success would not be possible, he withdrew and settled in Fukuiura, Izumi Province. Sonabe Hebei Tadayasu, a resident of Kii Province, also attempted to turn his back on the Taira and serve the Minamoto; however, when he heard that Yasumasa Rokuro had been attacked by Lord Tono and had taken refuge in Fukui, he gathered a force of approximately one hundred horsemen and joined forces with him. As Lord Tono immediately followed up with an attack, they defended for a day and a night. Yasumasa Rokuro and Sonabe Hebei, thinking that success would not be possible, ordered their retainers to shoot defense arrows while they themselves escaped to the capital. text: 同二月四日、福原には故入道相國の忌日とて、佛事形の如く行はる。朝夕の軍立に過行く月日は知らね共、去年は今年に回り來て、憂かりし春にも成にけり。世の世にて有ましかば、如何なる起立塔婆の企、供佛施僧の營みも有べかりしかども、唯男女の君達指し聚ひて、泣より外の事ぞなき。

annotation.translation: On the fourth day of the same second month, at Fuhara, because it was the anniversary of the deceased Retired Emperor, a Buddhist ceremony was held as usual. Although the passing days and months have gone by in the midst of military preparations, last year has come to turn into this year, and it has become a sorrowful spring. If the world had remained as it was, there would surely have been plans for building memorial pagodas and arrangements for offering food to the Buddha and alms to monks; but now, the lords and ladies merely gather together, and there is nothing to be done but weep.

annotation.translation: When it was heard that the Taira had already advanced to Fukuhara and were returning to the capital, the people who remained in their native places were neither happy nor joyful. Nii no Sōzu Senchin, because he had been the Taira's guest at Kajii-no-miya for many years, was told of this by wind of news. The Prince also usually sent word: 'The state of the sky on a journey is indeed distressing to think upon. Even the capital is not at peace.' Among other things, he wrote, there was a poem in the inner room.

text: さる程に小松三位中將維盛卿は、年隔り日重るに隨ひて、故郷に留め置給ひし北の方少き人々の事をのみ歎き悲み給ひけり。商人の便に、おのづから文などの通ふにも、北方の都の御在樣、心苦う聞給ふに、さらば迎へとて、一所でいかにも成らばやとは思へども、我身こそあらめ、人の爲痛くてなど、思召し忍びて、明し暮し給ふにこそ、責ての志の深さの程も露れけれ。

annotation.translation: In this manner, Prince Taira no Tomomori, the Third Rank of Komatsu, as the years grew apart and piled upon one another, sighed and lamented only about the young people in the north who had been left behind in his hometown. When letters naturally came through the merchants, he would feel uneasy hearing about the appearance of the Emperor in the capital of the north; yet, though he thought, 'If only I could gather them all in one place,' he would bear his own suffering and the pain of others, thinking, 'I must endure,' and spend his days and nights, and thus the depth of his resolve became revealed.

text: 平家の方には大將軍小松新三位中將資盛、同少將有盛、丹後侍從忠房、備中守師盛、侍大將には平内兵衞清家、海老次郎盛方を初として、都合其勢三千餘騎、小野原より三里隔てゝ三草山の西の山口に陣をとる。其夜の戌の刻ばかり、九郎御曹司、土肥次郎を召て、「平家は是より三里隔てて、三草山の西の山口に、大勢で引へたんなるは今夜夜討によすべきか、明日の軍か」と宣へば、田代冠者進み出でて申けるは、「明日の軍と延られなば、平家勢附候なんず。平家は三千餘騎、御方の御勢は一萬餘騎、遙の利に候。夜討好んぬと覺候。」と申ければ、土肥次郎、「いしうも申させ給ふ田代殿哉。さらば軈て寄せさせ給へ。」とて打立けり。兵共「暗さは暗し、如何せんずる。」と口々に申ければ、九郎御曹司「例の大たいまつは如何に。」と宣まへば、土肥次郎「さる事候。」とて、小野原の在家に火をぞ懸たりける。是を始て、野にも山にも草にも木にも火を付たれば、晝にはちとも劣らずして、三里の山をこえゆきけり。

annotation.translation: On the Heike side, the great general Komatsu no Shōsangi Nakashō Morimori, the same Shōgi Arimori, Tango no Zujō Tadafusa, Bitchū no Kami Mōmori, and on the side of the Shōtaishō, Hirauchi no Hyōe Kiyoyasu, Ebijirō Morihō, and others, totaling over three thousand horsemen, took up their positions at the western mountain pass of Mount Mikusa, three ri distant from Onohara. Around the hour of the dog on that night, the Ninth Prince summoned Tōi no Jirō and declared, "The Heike have retreated with a large force to the western mountain pass of Mount Mikusa, three ri distant from here. Shall we attack them tonight or tomorrow?" When this was said, Tashiro no Gon no Kami advanced and replied, "If we delay until tomorrow, the Heike forces will have arrived. The Heike number over three thousand horsemen, while our side has over ten thousand; we have a great advantage. It is better to attack by night." Hearing this, Tōi no Jirō said, "Indeed, Lord Tashiro speaks wisely. Then, let us advance at once." They immediately charged. The soldiers said one after another, "It is dark, what can we do?" When the Ninth Prince asked, "What of the usual large torches?" Tōi no Jirō replied, "Such things are prepared." Then they set fire to the dwellings in Onohara. From that time on, they set fire to fields, mountains, grass, and trees, so that by day it was no less bright than night, and they crossed the three-ri mountain.

text: 此田代冠者と申は、父は伊豆國の先の國司、中納言爲綱の末葉也。母は狩野介茂光が娘を思うて設たりしを、母方の祖父に預けて、弓矢取にはしたてたりけり。俗姓を尋ぬれば、後三條院の第三の王子、資仁親王より五代の孫也。俗姓も好き上、弓矢を取ても好りけり。

annotation.translation: This man of the Tashiro family, who is called the Crown Prince, is the descendant of the provincial governor of Izumi Province, the Middle Counselor Takanori. His mother was the daughter of Kano no Suke Shigemitsu, whom he left in the care of his maternal grandfather and trained to be an archer. If one inquires into his common surname, he is the fifth-generation grandson of Prince Sanehito, the third son of Emperor Sanjo. He not only favored his common surname but also excelled in archery.

text: 平家の方には、其夜、夜討にせんずるをば知らずして、「軍は定めて明日の軍でぞ有んずらん。軍にも睡たいは大事の事ぞ。好う寢て軍せよ。」とて先陣は自用心するもありけれども、後陣の者ども、或は甲を枕にし、或は鎧の袖箙などを枕にして、先後も知らずぞ臥たりける。夜半ばかりに、源氏一萬騎、おしよせて、鬨をどと作る。平家の方には、餘りに遽噪いで、弓取る者は矢を知らず、矢取る者は弓を知らず、馬に當られじと中を明てぞ通しける。源氏は落行く敵をあそこに追懸け、こゝに追詰め攻ければ、平家の軍兵矢庭に五百餘騎討れぬ。手負者ども多かりけり。大將軍小松新三位中將、同少將、丹後侍從、面目なうや思はれけん、播磨國高砂より舟に乘て、讃岐の八島へ渡給ひぬ。備中守は平内兵衞海老次郎を召具して、一谷へぞ參られける。

annotation.translation: On the Heike side, they did not know that an attack would be launched that night, saying, 'The enemy army will surely attack tomorrow. In any army, sleep is a matter of great importance. Sleep well and fight.' Thus, while the vanguard, though they tried to keep watch, lay down, the rear guard either used their armor as a pillow or their breastplates and sleeves as pillows, not caring whether they were in the front or rear, and lay down. Around midnight, ten thousand men of the Minamoto came surging forward and raised a great shout. On the Heike side, in the great commotion, those who reached for their bows did not know how to use them, and those who reached for their arrows did not know how to use them; they opened the center and rushed through, thinking to avoid being struck by horses. The Minamoto pursued the retreating enemy here and there, pressing the attack, and over five hundred riders of the Heike army were killed in the midst of the battlefield. Many were wounded. The Great General, Komatsu no Shinsanmi no Shunagon, along with the Junior Shunagon and Tango no Shijun, perhaps thinking it shameful, took to a boat from Takasago in Harima Province and crossed over to Yashima in Sanuki Province. Bitchū no Kami summoned Hirauchi no Buei Ebijirō and went to Hitotani.

text: 大臣殿は安藝右馬助能行を使者で、平家の君達の方々へ、「九郎義經こそ三草の手を責落いて、既に亂入候なれ。山の手は大事に候。各向はれ候へ。」と宣ひければ、皆辭し申されけり。能登殿の許へ、「度々の事で候へども、御邊向はれ候なんや。」と、宣ひ遣されたりければ、能登殿の返事には「軍をば我身一つの大事ぞと思うてこそ好う候へ。獵漁などの樣に、足立ちの好らう方へは向はん、惡からん方へは向はじなど候はんには、軍に勝つ事よも候はじ。幾度でも候へ、強からん方へは教經承はて、向ひ候はん。一方ばかりは打破り候べし。御心安う思召され候へ。」と憑し氣にぞ申されける。大臣殿斜ならず悦で、越中前司盛俊を先として、能登殿に一萬餘騎をぞ附られける。兄の越前三位通盛卿相具して、山の手をぞ固め給ふ。山の手と申は、鵯越の麓也。通盛卿は能登殿の假屋に、北方迎へ奉て、最後の名殘惜まれけり。能登殿大に怒て、「此手は強い方とて、教經を向けられて候也。誠に強う候べし。唯今も上の山より源氏さと落し候なば、取る物も取あへ候はじ。縱弓を持たりとも、矢を番ずば叶ひがたし。縱矢を番たりとも、引ずば猶惡かるべし。ましてさ樣に打解させ給ては、何の用にか立せ給ふべき。」と諫められて、げにもと思はれけん、急ぎ物具して、人をば歸し給ひけり。五日の暮方に、源氏昆陽野を立て、漸々生田森に攻近づく。雀松原、御影の松、昆陽野の方を見渡せば、源氏手々に陣を取て、遠火を燒く。深行まゝに眺むれば山の端出る月の如し。平家も「遠火燒や。」とて、生田森にも形の如くぞ燒たりける。明行まゝに見渡せば晴たる空の星の如し。是や昔河邊の螢と詠じ給ひけんも、今こそ思ひ知れけれ。源氏は、あそこに陣取て馬休め、こゝに陣取て馬飼などしける程に急がず。平家の方には「今や寄する、今や寄する。」と安い心も無りけり。

annotation.translation: The Minister sent Aki no Umasuke Yoruyuki as an envoy to the Heike lords, saying, 'It was Goemon Yoshitsune who struck down the hands at Sanjo, and he has already intruded. The mountain pass is critical. Please advance accordingly.' All of them refused. When he was sent to the house of the Lord of Noto, saying, 'Although it has happened many times, please advance to your side,' the Lord of Noto replied with a determined spirit: 'I consider the army as my sole concern; it would be good if I thought so. Just as in hunting or fishing, I would advance to the side where the footing is good, and I would not advance to the side where the footing is bad. If I were to think that, the army would never win. No matter how many times it happens, I, Yoritsune, will not retreat to the strong side and will advance. One side must be broken. Please think calmly.' The Minister was not displeased but delighted. He made Echizen no Matsu-kyo Morotoshi his vanguard and attached more than ten thousand cavalry to the Lord of Noto. His brother, Echizen no Sanmi Michimori, gathered his forces and fortified the mountain pass. The mountain pass refers to the foot of the Shiratori Pass. Michimori went to the temporary house of the Lord of Noto in the north, greeted him, and regretted the final farewell. The Lord of Noto became greatly angry and said, 'This side is the strong side, and Yoshitsune has been directed against it. It is certainly strong. Even now, if the Genji were to descend from the upper mountain, there would be nothing left to capture. Even if they hold their bows, they could not nock their arrows. Even if they nock their arrows, they could not draw them; it would still be difficult. Moreover, if you were to break through like this, for what purpose would you stand?' He was advised, and it seems he thought, 'Indeed,' so he quickly prepared his equipment and sent the people back. At dusk on the fifth day, the Genji took Kunoyano and gradually advanced toward Ikuta-mori. Looking over Suzumatsu-hara, the Pine of the Imperial Image, and toward Kunoyano, the Genji had set up camps in every direction and lit distant fires. Gazing deeply, it was like the moon rising from the edge of the mountain. The Heike also said, 'Light the distant fires,' and set fires in Ikuta-mori in the same manner. Looking as the day brightened, it was like the stars in the clear sky. Is this the firefly of the riverbank that was sung of in ancient times? Now I truly understand. The Genji, having set up camp there and resting their horses, and having set up camp here and feeding their horses, did not rush. On the Heike side, there was no thought of 'Now they are approaching, now they are approaching.'"

text: 六日の明ぼのに、九郎御曹司、一萬餘騎を二手に分け、先づ土肥次郎實平をば七千餘騎で一谷の西の手へ差遣はす。我身は三千餘騎で、一谷のうしろ鵯越を落さんと、丹波路より搦手にこそまはられけれ。兵共「是は聞ゆる惡所で有なり。同う死ぬるとも敵に逢うてこそ死たけれ惡所に落ては死たからず。あはれ此山の案内者やあるらん。」と面々に申ければ、武藏國の住人平山武者所進み出でて、申けるは、「季重こそ案内は知て候へ。」御曹司、「和殿は東國生立の者の、今日始めて見る西國の山の案内者、大に實しからず。」と宣へば、平山重ねて申けるは、「御諚とも覺候はぬ者哉。吉野泊瀬の花をば歌人が知り、敵の籠たる城の後の案内をば剛の者が知候。」と申ければ、是又傍若無人にぞ聞えける。

annotation.translation: On the sixth day, at dawn, the young lord Kyūgo divided his force of more than ten thousand cavalry into two divisions, first dispatching Tōi Jirō Sanehei with more than seven thousand cavalry to the western flank of Iwaya. He himself, with more than three thousand cavalry, intended to descend from Hyōryōgōe behind Iwaya and approach from the rear via the Tamba route. The soldiers said, "This is the infamous place of which we have heard. Even if we must die together, we would rather die meeting the enemy than die in such a treacherous place. Is there perhaps a guide for this mountain?" Each man spoke his mind. Then, a resident of Musashi Province, Hira-yama Musha-dokoro, stepped forward and said, "Hira-yama knows the way." The young lord replied, "Wadono is a man born in the Eastern Provinces; a guide from the Western Provinces whom he has seen for the first time today is not sufficiently reliable." Hira-yama then reiterated, "Do you not understand that this is your command? The poets know the flowers of Yoshino and Pose, but the strong know the way behind the enemy's fortress." This was heard as yet another instance of his audacity.

text: 又武藏國の住人別府小太郎清重とて、生年十八歳に成る小冠者進出て申けるは、「父で候し義重法師が教候しは、『敵にも襲はれよ、又山越の狩をもせよ、深山に迷ひたらん時は、老馬に手綱を打懸て、先に追立て行け、必道へ出うずるぞ。』とこそ教候しか。」御曹司、「優うも申たる者哉。雪は野原を埋めども、老たる馬ぞ道は知ると云ふ樣有り。」とて、白葦毛なる老馬に鏡鞍置き、白轡はげ、手綱結で打懸け、先に追立て、未知ぬ深山へこそ入給へ。比は二月初の事なれば、峯の雪村消て、花かと見ゆる所も有り。谷の鶯音信て、霞に迷ふ所も有り。上れば白雪皓々として聳え、下れば青山峨々として岸高し。松の雪だに消やらで、苔の細道幽なり。嵐にたぐふ折々は、梅花とも又疑はれ、東西に鞭を上、駒をはやめて行く程に、山路に日暮ぬれば、皆下居て陣をとる。武藏坊辨慶、老翁を一人具して參りたり。御曹司、「あれは何者ぞ。」と問たまへば、「此山の獵師で候。」と申。「さて案内は知たるらん。在の儘に申せ。」とこそ宣ひけれ。「爭か存知仕らで候べき。」「是より平家の城廓一谷へ落さんと思ふは如何に。」「努々叶ひ候まじ。三十丈の谷十五丈の岩崎など申處は人の通べき樣候はず。まして御馬などは思ひも寄り候はず。其うへ城のうちにはおとしあなをもほり、ひしをもうゑて待まゐらせ候らんと申。」「さてさ樣の所は鹿は通ふか。」「鹿は通ひ候。世間だにも暖に成候へば、草の深いに臥うとて、播磨の鹿は丹波へ越え、世間だにも寒う成り候へば、雪の淺きに食んとて、丹波の鹿は播磨の印南野へかよひ候。」と申。御曹司「さては馬場ごさんなれ。鹿の通はう所を、馬の通はぬ樣や有る。軈て汝案内者つかまつれ。」とぞ宣ひける。此身は年老て叶うまじい由を申す。「汝は子は無か。」「候」とて、熊王と云童の生年十八歳になるをたてまつる。やがて髻取あげ父をば鷲尾庄司武久と云ふ間、是をば鷲尾三郎義久と名乘せ、先打せさせて、案内者にこそ具せられけれ。平家追討の後、鎌倉殿に中違うて、奧州で討れ給ひし時鷲尾三郎義久とて、一所で死ける兵也。

annotation.translation: There was also a resident of Musashi Province named Betpu no Kotaro Kiyeshige, who had just turned eighteen years old. He stepped forward and said, 'My father, the priest Yoshishige, instructed me thus: "Even if the enemy attacks, or you engage in mountain hunting, if you become lost in the deep mountains, strike the reins of an old horse, urge it on ahead, and you will surely find the road."' The noble lord said, 'Truly, he has spoken well. Although the snow fills the fields, it is said that even an old horse knows the way.' Thus, he placed a mirror saddle upon a white horse, put on white bridle straps, tied and struck the reins, urged the horse on ahead, and entered the unknown deep mountains. Since this was in the early days of the second month, the snow on the peaks had melted, and there were places that appeared like flowers. In the valleys, the sound of the cuckoo could be heard, and there were places where one became lost in the mist. Ascending, the white snow stood high and brilliant; descending, the green mountains rose steeply and their banks were high. Even the snow upon the pines had not yet melted, and the mossy narrow paths were secluded. At times resembling a storm, the plum blossoms might be mistaken for snow. As they whipped their horses and rode east and west, when the sun set upon the mountain path, they all descended and established a camp. Musashi-bo Benkei had accompanied a single old man. The noble lord asked, 'Who is that?' The old man replied, 'I am a hunter of this mountain.' The lord said, 'Then you must know the way here. Speak as you are.' The old man said, 'I do not know it at all.' The lord asked, 'What do you think if we descend from here to the Heike castle at Hitotani?' The old man replied, 'It will certainly not be possible. There are places such as the thirty-jō deep valley and the fifteen-jō high rocky ridge where no one can pass, let alone horses. Furthermore, within the castle they have dug hidden traps and set up lances to await us.' The lord asked, 'Then can deer pass through such places?' The old man replied, 'Deer do pass. When the world becomes warm, deer lie down in the deep grass, and deer from Harima cross to Tanba; when the world becomes cold, they go to eat in the shallow snow, and deer from Tanba visit Inami-no in Harima.' The lord said, 'Then it is a horse path. Can there be a place where deer pass but horses do not? Soon, you shall serve as my guide.' The old man said that it was impossible for him due to his old age. The lord asked, 'Do you have a child?' The old man replied, 'Yes,' and presented a boy named Kumao, who was eighteen years old. They immediately untied his topknot; the father was named Washio no Shoji Takehisa, and this one was given the name Washio no Saburo Yoshihisa, and he was made to lead the way as a guide. After the pursuit and destruction of the Heike, when he served the Lord of Kamakura and was killed in the province of Mutsu, he was known as Washio no Saburo Yoshihisa, a soldier who died together with him.

text: 六日の夜半ばかりまでは、熊谷平山搦手にぞ候ける。熊谷次郎、子息の小次郎を喚で云けるは、「此手は惡所を落さんずる時に、誰先といふ事も有まじ。いざうれ是より土肥が承はて向うたる播磨路へ向うて、一谷の眞先懸う。」と云ひければ、小次郎、「然べう候。直家もかうこそ申たう候つれ。さらばやがて寄せさせ給へ。」と申す。熊谷、「誠や平山も此手にあるぞかし、打込の軍好まぬ者也。平山が樣見て參れ。」とて、下人を遣はす。案の如く平山は、熊谷より先に出立て、「人をば知らず、季重に於ては一引も引まじい者を。」と、獨り言をぞし居たりける。下人が馬を飼ふとて、「憎い馬の長食哉。」とて、打ければ、「かうなせそ、其馬の名殘も、今夜ばかりぞ。」とて打立けり。下人走歸て、急ぎ此由告たりければ、「さればこそ。」とて、やがて是も打出けり。熊谷は、かちの直垂に、赤革威の鎧著て、紅の母衣を懸け、ごんだ栗毛と云ふ聞ゆる名馬にぞ乘たりける。小次郎は、澤潟を一しほすたる直垂に、節繩目の鎧著て、西樓と云ふ白月毛なる馬に乘たりけり。旗差はきぢんの直垂に、小櫻を黄にかへいたる鎧著て、黄河原毛なる馬にぞ乘たりける。落さんずる谷をば弓手になし、馬手へ歩ませゆく程に、年比人も通はぬ田井の畑と云ふ古道を經て、一谷の波打際へぞ出たりける。一谷の近く鹽屋と云ふ處に未だ夜深かりければ、土肥次郎實平、七千餘騎で引へたり。熊谷は波打際より夜に紛て、そこをつと打通り、一谷の西の木戸口にぞ押寄たる。其時は未だ夜ふかゝりければ敵の方にも靜返て音もせず。御方一騎もつゞかず。熊谷次郎子息の小次郎を喚で云ひけるは、「我も／＼と先に心を懸たる人々は多かるらん。心狹う直實計とは思ふべからず。既に寄せたれども、未だ夜の明るを相待て、此邊にも引へたるらん。いざ名乘う。」とて、掻楯の際に歩ませ寄り、大音聲を揚て、「武藏國の住人熊谷次郎直實、子息の小次郎直家、一谷の先陣ぞや。」とぞ名乘たる。平家の方には、「よし／＼音なせそ。敵に馬の足を疲かせよ。矢種をば射盡させよ。」とて、會釋ふ者も無りけり。

annotation.translation: Until about midnight of the sixth day, Kumaigai was stationed at the rear guard of Taira no Shirohei. Kumaigai summoned his son, Kojirō, and said, 'When retreating from a difficult position, there is no question of who goes first. Come now, let us proceed from here, through Tōi, to the Harima road, and be the first to charge into Ichinotani.' Kojirō replied, 'That is proper. My father also said just so. Then, please order the troops to advance at once.' Kumaigai said, 'Indeed, Taira no Shirohei is likely in this position. The sudden attack is not to his liking. Have someone go and take a look.' So he sent a servant. As expected, Shirohei had already set out ahead of Kumaigai, muttering to himself, 'A man who does not retreat even one step in the face of adversity.' The servant, pretending to tend the horse, said, 'What a hateful horse, so greedy for food,' and struck it. The horse cried out, 'Do not do this! Even the memory of this horse will be gone by tonight,' and collapsed. The servant ran back and quickly reported what had happened. 'Then so be it,' he said, and immediately ordered the troops to advance. Kumaigai was wearing a crimson-colored direct-hanging armor, a lacquered leather cuirass, and a red momoe; he was mounted on a famous horse named 'Gonda Kurage.' Kojirō wore a direct-hanging armor dyed with water plantain, a cuirass with knotted cords, and rode a white horse named 'Seirō.' The banner bearer wore a direct-hanging armor of dried grass, a cuirass with small cherry blossoms dyed yellow, and rode a horse named 'Kōkōbara.' They turned the valley they were about to abandon into a bow-hand position and, as the horsemen began to walk forward, they passed through an ancient road called 'Taino no Hatake,' a path not even traversed by people in previous years, and emerged at the shoreline of Ichinotani. Near Ichinotani, at a place called Shiroya, it was still late at night, so Taira no Tōi Jirō Sanemori held back with over seven thousand cavalry. Kumaigai, from the shoreline, slipped through the night and pressed forward to the western gate of Ichinotani. At that time, it was still late at night, and on the enemy's side, there was no sound or movement. Not a single rider from our side followed. Kumaigai summoned his son, Kojirō, and said, 'There are surely many who would have taken the initiative earlier. Do not think that I am narrow-minded. Although we have advanced, they may still be waiting for the night to grow brighter before retreating from this area. Come, let us announce our names.' So, advancing to the edge of the shield, he raised his voice and proclaimed, 'I am Kumagai no Jirō Naokane, a resident of Musashi Province, and my son, Kojirō Naie. We are the vanguard at Ichinotani!' On the side of the Taira clan, they said, 'Good! Do not make any noise. Let us tire the enemy's horses. Let us exhaust their arrows.' Thus, there was no one to answer.

text: さる程に又後に武者こそ一騎續いたれ。「誰そ。」と問へば「季重」と答ふ。「問は誰そ。」「直實ぞかし。」「如何に熊谷殿はいつよりぞ。」「直實は宵よりよ。」とぞ答へける。「季重もやがて續て寄べかりけるを、成田五郎に謀れて、今迄遲々したる也。成田が死ば一所で死なうと契る間、『去らば。』とて打連寄る間『痛う平山殿、先懸早りなし給ひそ。先きを蒐ると云は、御方の勢を後に置て、蒐たればこそ、高名不覺も人に知るれ。唯一騎大勢の中にかけ入て討れたらんは、何の詮か在んずるぞ。』と制する間、げにもと思ひ、小坂の有るを先に打上せ、馬の首を下樣に引立て、御方の勢をまつ處に、成田も續て出來たり、打竝て軍の樣をも言合せんずるかと思ひたれば、さはなくて、季重をばすげなげに打見て、やがてつと馳拔通る間、あはれ此者は謀て、先懸けうとしけるよと思ひ、五六段ばかり先立たるを、あれが馬は我馬よりは弱げなる者をと目をかけ、一もみもうで追著て、『正なうも季重程の者をば謀り給ふ者哉。』と言ひかけ、打捨て寄つれば、遙に下りぬらん、よも後影をも見たらじ。」とぞ云ひける。

annotation.translation: In this manner, later on, a warrior followed in single file. 'Who is it?' was asked, and 'Kishigeyo' was answered. 'Who asks?' 'Naotane, indeed.' 'How long has Kumagai been on this?' 'Naotene since evening.' Thus he answered. 'Kishigeyo was also soon to follow and draw near, but he was betrayed by Narita Gorō and has been lingering thus far. Since he promised to die together with Narita, saying, 'If you go,' and was being struck and driven on, saying, 'Painful, Lord Hirayama, do not hasten the vanguard. To gather ahead means leaving your lord's ranks behind; only by gathering thus did even the renowned and unsuspecting become known to men. If one warrior, alone, were to charge into a vast host and be slain, what purpose would that serve?' Thus he restrained him. 'Indeed,' he thought, 'I shall raise the pole of the small hill first, pull the horse's head down, and wait for my lord's forces. I thought that Narita would also come forth and draw near, so that we might speak together of the army's appearance.' But that was not the case. Kishigeyo was struck down without hesitation, and as he quickly spurred his horse and passed through, 'Alas, this man has plotted to make a false vanguard,' he thought. Seeing that he had advanced some five or six ranks ahead, he thought, 'His horse is weaker than mine,' and fixed his eyes on him, chasing with all his might, saying, 'Surely, is there anyone who would plot against a man like Kishigeyo?' and then let him go, thinking, 'He will surely fall far behind; he will not even be seen from behind.'
